effect_estimate.comment: Note minor internal discrepancy in the paper's text vs. Table 5 on PDF p. 11: the prose reports WTAC of $4.19/hour and $29.10/additional outage and WTP of $0.15/hour and $4.05/outage, whereas Table 5 prints WTAC of $4.19/hour and $41.18/occurrence and WTP of $1.45/hour and $7.95/occurrence, and labels the $9.37 WTAC implicit price as 'Alternative supply arrangements' while the text on p. 12 identifies $9.37 as 'information only if you phoned in'. Both sets of printed figures are reported here for completeness.
effect_estimate.value: In multinomial probit models comparing consumer property-rights framing via one-off water bill rebates (WTAC, N = 1,321 choice observations, chi-square = 52.07, p < 0.01) against utility property-rights framing via annual water rate increases (WTP, N = 1,111 choice observations, chi-square = 160.63, p < 0.01), respondents valued a broader range of customer service attributes under WTAC than under WTP. Under WTP, only annual water rate increases (beta = -0.064, t = -11.390, p < 0.01), interruption duration (beta = 0.093, t = 2.560, p < 0.01), and interruption frequency (beta = 0.507, t = 2.910, p < 0.01) were statistically significant, whereas communication and alternative supply were not significant; implicit WTP prices were $1.45/hour in Table 5 ($0.15/hour in text) to reduce outage duration and $7.95/occurrence in Table 5 ($4.05 in text) to reduce annual outages. Under WTAC, bill rebates (beta = 0.014, t = 4.754, p < 0.01), outage duration (beta = -0.059, t = -1.978, p < 0.05), outage frequency (beta = -0.578, t = -3.833, p < 0.01), radio announcement notification (beta = -0.130, t = -2.049, p < 0.05), and phone-in-only notification (beta = -0.131, t = -1.843, p < 0.10) were all significant, yielding implicit WTAC compensation prices of $4.19 per additional outage hour, $41.18 in Table 5 ($29.10 in text) per additional annual outage, $9.24 for radio announcement in place of a letterbox card, and $9.37 for phone-in-only information (labelled 'Alternative supply arrangements' in Table 5).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped by the cross-sectional observational survey design ceiling (<= 2) and rated 1 because the study documents statistical associations in a hypothetical stated-preference choice experiment comparing property-rights/rebate vs. rate-increase framings, without directly observing an actual legal or administrative customer-service-standard/rebate regime operating on real-world water service delivery.

sample_size.comment: 80.1% survey response rate (669 completed out of 835 households contacted from stratified street-interruption sampling frame; 75 refusals and 91 uncompleted pickups). Each respondent was given 6 choice tasks; after excluding 'Don't know' and missing responses, the estimated multinomial probit models used N = 1,321 WTAC and N = 1,111 WTP choice observations.
sample_size.value: 669 completed household surveys (out of 835 randomly drawn households contacted; 332 willingness-to-accept-compensation surveys and 337 willingness-to-pay surveys); 2,432 analyzed choice observations in multinomial probit models (N = 1,321 WTAC observations; N = 1,111 WTP observations)

study_design.comment: Drop-off-pick-up cross-sectional stated-preference household survey in streets with >= 3 water interruptions over 2 years, using an experimental fractional factorial design (192 choice sets in 32 blocks of 6 choice tasks) to compare WTAC (rebate) and WTP (annual bill increase) framings via simulated maximum likelihood multinomial probit models.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional stated-preference household survey using discrete choice modelling (split-sample willingness-to-accept-compensation vs. willingness-to-pay choice sets) analyzed with multinomial probit regression
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 4, Section 2; PDF pp. 4-9, Sections 3-5
